stories.text: George Fitzroy Seymour owned the estate from 1949 to 1994, and Miranda Seymour has owned it since.

The hall came to the Byrons when George Byron, 8th Baron Byron, married Lucy Wescomb in 1843, and they kept it for about a hundred years. Frederick, the 10th Baron, was the village's vicar and from 1917 its squire as well: its "squarson".

The Pigot family built Thrumpton Hall in rose-coloured brick, and it was largely complete by 1617. In the 1660s Gervase Pigot altered and improved it. Its Jacobean cantilevered staircase was carved from the estate's own timber, with John Webb, a pupil of Inigo Jones, overseeing the work.

The Powdrells, a Roman Catholic family, had a house here, which they lost after the Babington Plot. Around it the Pigots built a rose-brick house, largely complete by 1617. Part of the Powdrells' house survives inside it, with a priest hole.

19862.sum: Thrumpton Hall is an English country house in the village of Thrumpton near Nottingham. It operated as a wedding venue until November 2020.

stories.text: The red-brick dovecote on the green was built in the early 18th century for the Clifton family's farming estate.[^cvra] It is said to be one of the largest in England, with about 2,300 nesting places; pigeons were kept for winter meat.[^walk] A stone tablet on its side remembers the men of the village who died in the First World War.[^roll] It is listed Grade II.

stories.text: The Clifton family held the manor of Clifton from the late 13th century, and this was their manor house.[^s1] Sir Gervase Clifton largely rebuilt it between 1778 and 1797, partly to designs by John Carr of York.[^s1] In 1958 the family sold it, ending 700 years of ownership; it became a girls' grammar school, and is now two houses.[^s1] The hall itself dates from the late 16th century and is listed Grade I. In its grounds are a brick ice house of the mid-18th century, the vaulted remains of a curved garden stairway, a pair of Coade stone lions of the early 19th century, and the late 18th-century stable block, now cottages.[^s2]

stories.text:
The house was designed in 1781 for the Smith family as Wilford Hall, the centre of an estate with stables, lodges for the house staff and a private chapel.[^walk] It is a red-brick country house of three storeys and five bays, listed Grade II, and its stable block of the same year is listed too. The Smiths' bank in Nottingham is believed to have been the first bank outside London, and Samuel Smith, an MP for 44 years, is believed to have built the house; by 1790 it was his.[^throsby] The banker Abel Smith died at Wilford on 12 July 1788.[^s1][^s2] His wife's younger sister, Elizabeth Bird, was the mother of William Wilberforce, the slavery abolitionist, who stayed at the house for several months between 1786 and 1789.[^s1][^s2][^s3] In 1853 it was the seat of Henry Smith, a large, handsome brick mansion; he owned about 70 acres of the parish, and in 1828 he built an infant school in the village.[^white]

Thomas Forman, who founded the Nottingham Post, later bought the house from the Smiths, and it passed to the Forman Hardy family; at some point it was renamed Wilford House.[^s1] It became offices in the 1980s, the Wilford Place estate was built on its grounds in 2006,[^trail] and in 2021 the house was given a multi-million pound refurbishment.[^s1]

dyk.text: Rioters burnt the Duke of Newcastle's mansion here in 1831, over his opposition to the Reform Bill. It reopened in 1878 as the first municipal art gallery in the UK outside London.

stories.text: When the House of Lords threw out the Second Reform Bill on 8 October 1831, rioting broke out in Nottingham and a crowd burned the castle, which belonged to the Duke of Newcastle, an opponent of reform. Three men were hanged; the Duke refused to restore the castle, and its burnt shell stood on the rock for years.

After Henry IV's queen, Joan of Navarre, lived here until 1437, the castle was little kept up, until the Wars of the Roses made it a stronghold again.[^s1] Edward IV proclaimed himself king in Nottingham, and in 1476 ordered a new tower and royal apartments, which John Leland, writing in 1540, thought the finest part of the castle.[^s1] On 20 August 1485 Richard III rode from Nottingham to Leicester, two days before he was killed at Bosworth.[^s2]

In 1643 Colonel John Hutchinson took command of Nottingham Castle, and Parliament later made him governor of both town and castle. It was a hard post: the town had no walls, the garrison was small and short of supplies, and the committee that ran the town quarrelled. Hutchinson held on all the same, and protected the radical separatists among his soldiers as far as he could.

The burnt mansion stood a ruin until Thomas Chambers Hine restored it in 1875. The Prince of Wales opened it in 1878 as Nottingham Castle Museum, the first municipal art gallery in the United Kingdom outside London. The castle closed in 2018 for a redevelopment that cost £30 million, and reopened on 21 June 2021 under the charity Nottingham Castle Trust. In November 2022 the trust said it was appointing liquidators, and the site went back to the council.

The first castle on the rock was a wooden motte-and-bailey, begun in 1068 on William the Conqueror's orders, and rebuilt in stone under Henry II. For centuries it was a royal fortress and an occasional royal residence. After the Civil War it was razed in 1651, and in the 1670s the 1st Duke of Newcastle began a mansion on the rock. Rioters burnt the mansion in 1831; it reopened as a museum in 1878.

The Royalists of Newark raided again and again. Sir Charles Lucas broke into the town in January 1644 and tried to set it on fire, and in April 1645 a party from Newark took the fort at Trent Bridge. Each time Hutchinson won back what was lost, and each demand that he surrender the castle he answered with fresh defiance.

A regiment raised in 1741 became, at the request of the people of Nottinghamshire, the 45th (1st Nottinghamshire) Regiment of Foot in 1779.[^s1] Against Napoleon it fought through the Peninsular War from 1808 to 1814, and at Talavera in 1809 won the nickname "Old Stubborns".[^s1] Renamed the Sherwood Foresters in 1866, it was joined with the Derbyshire regiment on 1 July 1881 as the Sherwood Foresters (Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire Regiment), whose museum is in the castle.[^s1]

Henry VIII sent new tapestries ahead of his visit in August 1511, but a survey of 1525 found the castle in "dekay and ruyne", part of the Great Hall's roof fallen in. It was garrisoned again in 1536, against the Pilgrimage of Grace, and in 1562 it was to host a meeting of Elizabeth I and Mary, Queen of Scots, which never took place. By 1600 it was no longer a royal home.

In 1995 the Design Museum in London put on True Brit, a show marking 25 years of the fashion business of Paul Smith, who was born in Beeston. It went on to Glasgow and then to his home city, where it was shown in Nottingham Castle.
Kate Watson Wallis (1852–1918), a suffragist, lived in the Residence at the Castle with her husband, the Castle Art Gallery's first curator.

In decline by the 16th century, the original castle, except for its walls and gates, was demolished after the English Civil War in 1651.

stories.text: Sir Francis Willoughby built Wollaton Hall between 1580 and 1588, probably to designs by the Elizabethan architect Robert Smythson. After a fire in 1642 the house stood empty for some forty years; Wyatville remodelled it from 1801. The 11th Baron Middleton sold it to Nottingham Corporation for £200,000, and since it opened to the public in 1926 it has held the city's natural history museum.
Cassandra Willoughby (1670–1735) oversaw the restoration of Wollaton Hall and its gardens.

83580.sum: Wollaton Hall is an Elizabethan country house of the 1580s standing on a small but prominent hill in Wollaton Park, Nottingham, England. The house is now Nottingham Natural History Museum, with Nottingham Industrial Museum in the outbuildings. The surrounding parkland has a herd of deer, and is regularly used for large-scale outdoor events such as rock concerts, sporting events and festivals.

stories.text: Papplewick Hall was built between 1781 and 1787 for the Hon. Frederick Montagu, and in 1795 the church of St James was built in its grounds.

175186.sum: Papplewick Hall is a Grade I listed English country house in Papplewick, Nottinghamshire.

stories.text: The first written record of a royal hunting lodge at Bestwood is from 1286, in the reign of Edward I. Charles II and Nell Gwyn visited it, and in 1682 he leased the lodge to her. Their son, Charles Beauclerk, Earl of Burford, was made Duke of St Albans in 1684, and Bestwood passed down through his descendants.

The present lodge was built in 1862–65 for the 10th Duke of St Albans by Samuel Sanders Teulon, in the Gothic Revival style. The army took it over in the Second World War, and in the mid-1970s it became a hotel. It is listed Grade II*.

179201.sum: Bestwood Lodge is a Grade II* listed 19th-century country house in the civil parish of Deer Park, Nottinghamshire, England. It was built in the Gothic Revival style in 1862–65 for the 10th Duke of St Albans by architect Samuel Sanders Teulon. It has been operated as the Bestwood Lodge Hotel since the 1970s.

stories.text: Henry Ashwell, a Basford bleacher, built Woodthorpe Grange in 1874. The council bought the house and grounds in 1921 for £15,000, Jesse Boot giving £5,000 of it, and the park opened in 1922.

stories.text: The Pierreponts held Holme from about 1280. Around 1500 the hall was built, one of the few brick houses of its time in Nottinghamshire. The family became Earls and Dukes of Kingston, then Earls Manvers, and the hall is listed Grade I.

Pierrepont is Norman French for "stone bridge". In 1257 Sir Henry Pierrepont married Annora de Manvers, heir to Holme, and the family stayed for almost seven centuries: Charles I made Sir Robert Pierrepont Earl of Kingston-upon-Hull in 1628, and George I made Evelyn Pierrepont a duke in 1715. The estate was broken up and sold in 1940.

291632.sum: Holme Pierrepont Hall is a medieval manor house located in the village of Holme Pierrepont, near Nottingham, Nottinghamshire, England. It is a Grade I listed building, recognised for its exceptional architectural and historical significance. Built between approximately 1490 and 1500 by Sir William Pierrepont, the hall is one of the few brick-built houses in Nottinghamshire from the period and remains in private ownership.

stories.text: In 1948 the Roman Catholic Diocese of Nottingham opened St Hugh's College at Tollerton Hall, a junior seminary for boys from 11. By 1969 it was taking boys who were not training for the priesthood, and it closed in 1986. The hall was then a company's headquarters until 2017, when it was bought as a private home again. It is listed Grade II.

317731.sum: St Hugh's College was a Roman Catholic minor seminary in Tollerton founded by the Diocese of Nottingham. The manor house dates to 1792, and the college was founded on the premises in 1948. It closed in 1986 and is a Grade II listed building.

stories.text: In 1860 Thomas Cross, a banker from Bolton, built the hall. From 1880 it was the home of Philo Laos Mills, an American merchant who became High Sheriff of Nottinghamshire. In the Second World War it became a hospital, and it stayed one until 1980.

319097.sum: Ruddington Hall is a country house standing in the grounds of a garden in Ruddington, Nottinghamshire, England. Ruddington Hall has been included in the art work of Nikolaus Pevsner alongside the Elizabethan Wollaton Hall and Newstead Abbey, ancestral home of Lord Byron. Pevsner described it as having a classical ethic of "calm grandeur, and monumental simplicity".
